chapter: Regional bands, politics and travel abroad
title: Rejecting a separate black nation: integration as the course of history
summary: Wilson says he rejected the Communist proposal of a southern black nation and argues the country is a melting pot heading toward integration.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Because they were making a big pitch for Negro support. But one thing, they lost me -- they had one proposition; they thought that the Negroes should segregate themselves into a southern nation, since the majority of the population of the south was Negro, in a majority vote, they would have their own black nation down South -- and I thought that was absolutely dead wrong, because this country was geared, since its inception, into an integration of all the nations of Europe and Asia and Africa, and the peoples of the earth -- that's the United States.
That's the whole point, psychologically and philosophically of the United States -- it's a melting pot of the earth. The Orient, Africa -- the Africans came

over here, they came over here as slaves in the beginning, but the English and the Spaniards and everything -- and the other people came over, the whites came over and got paid for their work, except the indentured slaves; they could work for a debt, and they were slaves for awhile, and then they became free -- but the Africans stayed slaves until the Civil War.

But still, those slaves built the country as much as the whites did from Spain and England and Germany or France, or wherever -- the foundation of the United States, they did the work, the country was built with work -- so that is, it is inevitable that it's going to be an integrated society, an integrated world. Any movement, the Communist movement, plugging back in the thirties for a separate black state in the South because the majority of the population was black -- it is counter to history. It's like the old prejudiced whites in the South; separate but equal. That's the thing that was overthrown by the Supreme Court in 1954, that separate business.

And besides, it's just slowing history up to fight for separatism anyway because the steamroller of history points to integration ... of everybody. You see it, people who have lived as long as we have, we've seen this process in our lifetime moving on its own, regardless of

what a person does in New York, what a person does in Paris or a person does in Birmingham, you see it in the relentless evolution of history, pulling people into one nation, regardless of what race -- or what your background is, whether you came from Africa, Asia or Europe.
